pack: Civic Leadership Legacy : The Institute Model
notes: The universal, state-agnostic edition of the Willie L. Brown Jr. Institute legacy training — leadership, civic duty, ethics AND emotional intelligence as one model, usable in any state or country via the eight-slot localizer (see docs/wiki/Legacy-Tracks.md). Where the state editions (Louisiana, California, Texas) localize, this pack teaches the model itself. DISCLAIMER, carried from the app: this track is a proposal built from the Willie L. Brown Jr. Institute of Politics and Public Service's public mission and the Fellowship Program at San Francisco State University. It is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or reviewed by the Institute, SF State, or Mayor Brown. 5 tracks x 10 themes x 5 grade bands = 250 blocks. Expanded by tools/generate_pack.py.

tracks.name: Leadership as service: the twelve principles in practice

themes.description: Public service taught as a craft with roles, crews, evidence and credentials — the founding principle, practiced rather than recited.
themes.transfer_check: Complete one documented act of public service where you live and present it to a real audience beyond your classroom or family.

bands.K–2: Help a classmate and tell an adult how it felt.
bands.3–5: Explain why helping others at school matters, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Explain why real public service is called a noble profession, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Reflect on a real act of public service you performed, on your own.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else why real public service deserves that description.

themes.theme: The leader's story as a text
themes.description: Reading a real public servant's record — the wins, the compromises, the record — as curriculum, not hagiography.
themes.transfer_check: Record a leader's-story interview with an experienced public servant and present its two most teachable decisions.

bands.K–2: Tell an adult a short story about someone who helped others.
bands.3–5: Read a simple story about a real leader, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Read a real leader's story and identify its lesson, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Analyse a real leader's story as a text with lessons to draw, on your own.
bands.11–12: Teach someone else how to read a real leader's story critically.

themes.description: The principle that a win that leaves people behind is unfinished — coalition maintenance as daily leadership work.
themes.transfer_check: For one real group decision you were part of, name who was at risk of being left behind and show what brought them along — or what should have.

bands.K–2: Invite a classmate who is left out to join a game, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Include someone who was left out of an activity, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Bring a real excluded person into a group activity, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Practice real inclusive leadership in a group you're part of, on your own.
bands.11–12: Teach someone else how to bring everyone along in a real group effort.

themes.description: Impact thinking: tracing who a decision touches before making it, with the wide-ranging-impacts principle as the discipline.
themes.transfer_check: Take one live local decision and map every group it touches, presenting the impact map before stating your own position.

bands.K–2: Think about how a choice affects a friend, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Consider how a real decision affects other people, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Weigh a real decision's effect on other real people, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Make a real decision that accounts for its effect on real lives, on your own.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else how to weigh a real decision's human cost.

themes.description: Being mentored and mentoring in both directions — the legacy chain as the model's transmission system.
themes.transfer_check: Establish one real mentoring link in each direction: a session where you learn from someone ahead, and one where you pass a skill behind.

bands.K–2: Help a younger student with something you know, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Mentor a younger student in something you're good at, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Mentor a real younger person in a real skill, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Mentor a real younger person while being mentored yourself, on your own.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else how a real mentorship chain sustains itself.

themes.description: Hands inside a real institution — why the model insists on placements, seminars and stipends rather than classroom civics alone.
themes.transfer_check: Complete a placement, shadow day or structured volunteer shift with a real public body, confirmed by a supervisor.

bands.K–2: Visit a real workplace with an adult and ask what people do there.
bands.3–5: Learn about a real job by visiting or asking, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Complete a real short placement or shadow at a real organisation, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Complete a real substantive placement at a real organisation, on your own.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else why a real placement teaches what a classroom cannot.

themes.description: The weekly cohort habit — field experience brought to a circle that questions it, reflection as part of the work.
themes.transfer_check: Run or take a speaking role in a seminar circle on a live local issue, presenting field evidence and taking questions on it.

bands.K–2: Sit in a circle and share an idea with classmates, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Discuss a real topic in a small group, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Participate in a real seminar-style discussion, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Lead a real seminar-style discussion on a real topic, on your own.
bands.11–12: Facilitate a real seminar circle that draws out quieter voices.

themes.description: The service ledger — hours, artifacts, references, credentials — evidence that opens doors, kept from the first act of service.
themes.transfer_check: Assemble your own service ledger to date in a form a scholarship or employer could verify.

bands.K–2: Keep a small folder of things you're proud of, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Keep a simple record of things you've done, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Build a real record of your own real activities and growth, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Build a real substantive record of your own leadership work, on your own.
bands.11–12: Advise someone else on building a real record that reflects their growth.

themes.description: Influence before office — organizing, convening and counting votes as a private citizen, where most leadership actually happens.
themes.transfer_check: Move one real small change without holding any position — document who you convened, what you asked, and what moved.

bands.K–2: Help organise a game without being asked, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Take initiative on a real group task without being asked, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Lead a real group effort without holding a formal title, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Lead a real group effort informally, without a title, on your own.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else how real leadership works without a title.

themes.theme: Living large: joy as a leadership discipline
themes.description: The twelfth principle — enjoying the work and sharing the joy — as sustainability, not indulgence.
themes.transfer_check: Identify what genuinely sustains you in service, schedule it into one real month of commitments, and report whether the work improved.

bands.K–2: Celebrate a small win with friends, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Celebrate a real group's success together, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Build real joy and celebration into a group's real work, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Practice real joy as a deliberate leadership discipline, on your own.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else why real joy is a leadership discipline, not a luxury.

tracks.name: The room and the count: coalition, negotiation, consensus

themes.description: The Speaker's craft generalized — knowing where every stakeholder stands before the meeting that decides.
themes.transfer_check: Before one real group decision, produce the written count — who is for, against, movable — and compare it to the outcome.

bands.K–2: Ask friends what they want before choosing a game, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Ask a group what they think before deciding, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Count real support for an idea before a real vote, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Count real support accurately before a real vote, on your own.
bands.11–12: Teach someone else how to count votes accurately before proposing something.

themes.description: Interests under positions — finding what an opponent must have, as distinct from what they say they want.
themes.transfer_check: In one real or role-played negotiation, state the other side's underlying interests to their satisfaction before proposing terms.

bands.K–2: Ask a friend why they want something different, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Ask what the other side of a disagreement actually wants, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Identify what a real opposing side actually needs, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Identify a real opposing side's real needs, on your own.
bands.11–12: Teach someone else how to find out what an opposing side genuinely needs.

themes.theme: The trade that makes the deal
themes.description: Log-rolling honestly — trading across issues so both sides win something they value more than what they give.
themes.transfer_check: Construct and close one real or simulated two-issue trade where both parties confirm they gained.

bands.K–2: Trade one toy for another fairly, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Make a fair trade with a friend, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Propose a real trade that makes a real deal possible, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Negotiate a real trade that closes a real deal, on your own.
bands.11–12: Teach someone else how to find the trade that actually makes a deal work.

themes.description: The tolerance principle — running a room where dissent improves the outcome instead of fracturing it.
themes.transfer_check: Chair one real discussion with genuine disagreement, and show where an opposing idea changed the final text.

bands.K–2: Listen to a different idea from a friend, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Consider an idea you disagree with, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Use a real opposing idea to strengthen a real group decision, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Incorporate real opposing ideas into a stronger real consensus, on your own.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else why real opposition strengthens real consensus.

themes.description: What gets discussed, in what order, decided by whom — agenda-setting as the quietest form of control, used transparently.
themes.transfer_check: Draft the agenda for one real meeting and annotate each ordering choice with the outcome it serves, shared openly with the group.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult who decides what a meeting talks about first.
bands.3–5: Notice that what's discussed first shapes a meeting, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Identify how a real agenda shapes a real meeting's outcome, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Set a real agenda that shapes a real meeting's outcome, on your own.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else why controlling the agenda is real power.

themes.description: Allies, opponents, persuadables and the unengaged — mapping a real issue's landscape before spending effort.
themes.transfer_check: Produce a coalition map for one concrete local change and have one person on it confirm their placement is accurate.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult who agrees with a friend's idea.
bands.3–5: Notice who supports a real idea and who doesn't, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Map a real coalition of support around an idea, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Build and map a real coalition around a real goal, on your own.
bands.11–12: Teach someone else how to map a real coalition of support.

themes.description: Keeping a coalition together under pressure — the maintenance calls, the credit sharing, the defection you see coming.
themes.transfer_check: For one real or case-study coalition, identify its most likely defector and design the specific move that keeps them.

bands.K–2: Keep a small group of friends agreeing on a game, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Keep a group agreeing on a plan even when it's shaky, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Hold together a real fragile group agreement, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Hold together a real fragile majority through a real decision, on your own.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else how to hold a real fragile majority together.

themes.description: The vote you lose — conceding without burning the room, and positioning for the next round.
themes.transfer_check: After a real or simulated loss, deliver the concession that keeps relationships and names the condition under which you return.

bands.K–2: Say something kind after losing a game, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Accept losing a game or vote gracefully, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Lose a real vote or decision gracefully, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Lose a real vote or decision gracefully, on your own.
bands.11–12: Teach someone else how to lose a real vote without damaging future work.

themes.description: Negotiating with an audience watching — what changes when the room has cameras, and what must never change.
themes.transfer_check: Run one negotiation twice — private and with observers — and report what the audience changed and what you refused to let it change.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult what happens when grown-ups negotiate in front of everyone.
bands.3–5: Watch a real negotiation happen in public, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Identify what makes a real public negotiation different, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Conduct a real negotiation with the public watching, on your own.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else the real pressures of negotiating in public.

themes.description: Writing agreements that survive — specificity, verification and the follow-through that makes the next deal possible.
themes.transfer_check: Draft one real agreement's terms so both sides can verify compliance, and check it against what actually happened after.

bands.K–2: Keep a promise you made to a friend, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Keep a real agreement you made with someone, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Make a real deal that both sides actually keep, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Structure a real deal so it actually holds over time, on your own.
bands.11–12: Teach someone else how to structure a real deal that lasts.

themes.description: Self-awareness under pressure — naming what you feel in the moment it starts steering you, before it speaks for you.
themes.transfer_check: Keep a one-week trigger log of real moments emotion started steering you, naming each feeling and what it wanted you to do.

bands.K–2: Name how you feel about something, with an adult's help.
bands.3–5: Notice and name your own feeling before reacting, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Identify your own real emotional state before acting, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Recognise your own real emotions before responding, on your own.
bands.11–12: Teach someone else how to read their own emotional state first.

themes.theme: The pause that saves the meeting
themes.description: Self-regulation — the practiced beat between provocation and response, and the techniques that create it.
themes.transfer_check: Demonstrate your pause technique in one real provocation — what you felt, what you did instead — verified by someone present.

bands.K–2: Take a breath before reacting to something upsetting, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Pause before responding to something frustrating, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Use a real pause to avoid a real bad reaction, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Use a real deliberate pause in a real tense moment, on your own.
bands.11–12: Teach someone else how a real pause can save a real meeting.

themes.description: Attunement at group scale — energy, alliances and unspoken objections read from faces, seating and silence.
themes.transfer_check: After one real meeting, write the room-read — who was with, against, checked out — and verify it with a participant.

bands.K–2: Notice if friends seem happy or upset, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Notice the mood of a group you're in, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Read a real room's mood accurately, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Read a real room's mood and adjust your approach, on your own.
bands.11–12: Teach someone else how to read a real room before speaking.

themes.description: Feeling with someone while still disagreeing — empathy as understanding, not capitulation.
themes.transfer_check: In one real disagreement, restate the other person's feeling and position to their satisfaction, then still state your own.

bands.K–2: Understand a friend's feelings without giving up your own idea, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Show empathy while still holding your own view, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Show real empathy without abandoning your real position, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Balance real empathy with holding your real position, on your own.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else the real difference between empathy and surrender.

themes.description: Bringing a hot person down — tone, space, acknowledgment — the sequence that works and the responses that inflame.
themes.transfer_check: Demonstrate the de-escalation sequence in one real or role-played confrontation through to a lowered temperature.

bands.K–2: Help calm down an upset friend, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Help calm a tense situation between friends, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: De-escalate a real tense situation, with a checker.
bands.9–10: De-escalate a real conflict on your own.
bands.11–12: Teach someone else real de-escalation technique for a tense moment.

themes.description: The emotion that signals injustice — feeling anger, extracting its information, and choosing its expression.
themes.transfer_check: Take one real thing that angers you, name the injustice inside it, and channel it into one constructive act, documented.

bands.K–2: Notice when you feel angry and tell an adult calmly.
bands.3–5: Express anger calmly instead of yelling, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Channel real anger productively in a real situation, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Use real anger productively without losing control, on your own.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else how real anger can be used well, not suppressed.

themes.description: Criticism, defeat and public embarrassment — absorbing hits without either collapse or counterattack.
themes.transfer_check: After one real piece of hard criticism, produce the sorted response: what was true, what was not, what you changed.

bands.K–2: Take a disappointment calmly with an adult's help.
bands.3–5: Handle real criticism or bad news calmly, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Receive real difficult news or criticism composedly, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Receive a real setback or criticism composedly, on your own.
bands.11–12: Teach someone else how to receive a real hard blow with composure.

themes.description: Naming the act, feeling its cost, changing the behavior — apology as repair work, not performance.
themes.transfer_check: Deliver one real apology that names the act and the cost, and report the changed behavior two weeks on.

bands.K–2: Say a real sorry that names what you did, with an adult's help.
bands.3–5: Write an apology that names what you did wrong, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Give a real apology that names the act and repairs harm, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Give a real apology that actually repairs real harm, on your own.
bands.11–12: Teach someone else what makes a real apology actually repair something.

themes.description: Who calms, who comforts, who absorbs — seeing the invisible emotional work in any team and distributing it deliberately.
themes.transfer_check: Map the emotional labor in one real group and redistribute one recurring piece of it, with the group's agreement.

bands.K–2: Help a friend feel better and ask someone else to help too, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Share the work of comforting others with a friend, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Share real emotional support work fairly within a group, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Share real emotional labor fairly in a group you lead, on your own.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else why real emotional labor needs to be shared fairly.

themes.description: The capstone: being the person a room stabilizes around in difficulty — composure as a practiced public skill.
themes.transfer_check: Hold the steady role through one real difficult event — meeting, emergency drill, hard conversation — with a witness's account of what you did.

bands.K–2: Stay calm when a friend is upset, with an adult nearby.
bands.3–5: Stay calm and steady when others are upset, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Provide a real steady presence during a real stressful moment, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Be a real steady presence for others during a real crisis, on your own.
bands.11–12: Teach someone else how to be a real steady presence under pressure.

themes.theme: The eight slots of any place
themes.description: The localizer as literacy — capital, legislature, local unit, standards, seal, industries, placements, partner — resolved for wherever you stand.
themes.transfer_check: Resolve all eight localization slots for your own state or country from official sources, on one page.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult who runs your town and what they do.
bands.3–5: Name one official who runs a real local place, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Identify the real key offices that govern any place, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Map the real eight key roles that govern any place, on your own.
bands.11–12: Teach someone else how to identify the real governing roles in any place.

themes.description: Local, state/provincial, national — what each actually does for the block you live on, wherever that is.
themes.transfer_check: For your own address, produce the who-does-what card: six common public matters each matched to the correct level and office.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult about the different levels of government.
bands.3–5: Name the different levels of government, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Identify a real issue and which government handles it, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Explain, for a real issue, which of your three governments handles it.
bands.11–12: Teach someone else how to identify which real government handles what.

themes.theme: The meeting that is open to you
themes.description: Open-meeting rules exist almost everywhere — finding the local body's schedule and taking the citizen's seat.
themes.transfer_check: Attend or watch one real public meeting of your local body and report one decision, who voted how, and who it affects.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult if regular people can go to town meetings.
bands.3–5: Learn that some government meetings are open to anyone, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Find a real open public meeting you could attend, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Attend a real open public meeting on your own.
bands.11–12: Guide someone else to a real open meeting relevant to their concern.

themes.description: Public-records rights in your jurisdiction — what is requestable, how, and the request done correctly.
themes.transfer_check: Submit or fully prepare one real public-records request under your jurisdiction's actual rules.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult if you can see a school's records.
bands.3–5: Learn that some government records are public, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Identify a real public record you could request, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Request a real public record on your own.
bands.11–12: Guide someone else through requesting a real public record.

themes.description: Registration, the ballot's shape and the down-ballot lines — your jurisdiction's actual voting machinery mastered.
themes.transfer_check: Verify a real registration and produce a plain-language guide to every line of your actual ballot's next election.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult how people vote in an election.
bands.3–5: Learn how a real person casts a vote, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Explain how a real citizen can vote from anywhere, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Explain, using real rules, how to vote wherever you live, on your own.
bands.11–12: Guide someone else through voting correctly wherever they are.

themes.theme: Speaking to power, on the record
themes.description: Public comment, testimony and the letter that gets answered — the citizen's formal voice in any system.
themes.transfer_check: Deliver (or fully rehearse to real rules) one formal public comment or submission to a real body on a live matter.

bands.K–2: Practice telling an adult your opinion clearly.
bands.3–5: Speak up about a real concern to an adult, with their help.
bands.6–8: Speak to a real official on the record, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Speak to a real official on the record, on your own.
bands.11–12: Coach someone else on speaking to real power effectively on the record.

themes.description: Civic information hygiene — verifying before repeating, correcting your own errors, and the transparency principle in daily speech.
themes.transfer_check: Fact-check three circulating civic claims against primary sources and publish the corrected versions where you first saw them.

bands.K–2: Tell the truth about what happened, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Describe a real event accurately, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Give a real accurate account of an event to an official, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Give real accurate testimony or public comment, on your own.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else why accuracy is a real civic duty.

themes.description: The duties that arrive by mail — jury service, the census, selective obligations — met as the system's load-bearing acts.
themes.transfer_check: For your jurisdiction, explain each summons-borne duty and simulate one — a mock deliberation to verdict, or a census-style enumeration done right.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult what a jury does in a courtroom.
bands.3–5: Learn what jury duty and the census are, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Identify a real civic duty like jury service or the census, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Fulfil a real civic duty like jury service or the census, on your own.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else why these real civic duties matter.

themes.description: The lowest rungs of elected and appointed office where you live — what they decide, what running requires.
themes.transfer_check: Identify three real entry-level offices or appointed seats open to someone like you, with each one's actual filing requirements.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult if a kid could ever be in charge of something.
bands.3–5: Learn about a real local office someone could run for, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Identify a real local office you could realistically run for, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Research a real local office and what running for it takes, on your own.
bands.11–12: Advise someone else on considering a real local office to run for.

themes.description: The affirmative principle localized — who has been blocked where you live, the data that shows it, and the push that is yours to make.
themes.transfer_check: Identify one barrier data shows still standing in your own community and complete one documented act that pushes against it.

bands.K–2: Try something a little hard and keep going, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Push past a real challenge in a group activity, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Identify a real barrier and push past it, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Push past a real limiting barrier in your own civic life, on your own.
bands.11–12: Help someone else push past a real ceiling they've hit.

themes.theme: What you see is what you get
themes.description: The transparency principle — removing the liability of hidden positions and moving on to the work.
themes.transfer_check: For one real matter where you hold an unpopular view, state it plainly to the relevant group and document what transparency cost and bought.

bands.K–2: Be honest about what actually happened, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Tell the truth even when it's hard, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Give a real honest account even when it's uncomfortable, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Give a real honest account of a real situation, on your own.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else why real transparency matters under pressure.

themes.description: Taking on what others dismiss — why the model insists on the cases nobody wants, and what taking one actually requires.
themes.transfer_check: Take one real dismissed case — a person, a request, a cause written off — and carry it one documented step further than anyone had.

bands.K–2: Keep trying to help even when it seems hard, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Keep helping in a real difficult situation, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Persist ethically in a real seemingly hopeless situation, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Act ethically in a real difficult, seemingly hopeless situation, on your own.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else how to act ethically in a real hopeless case.

themes.description: Seeing your own conflicts before others do — disclosure, recusal and the appearance that matters as much as the fact.
themes.transfer_check: Audit your own real roles for conflicts, disclose one properly in its actual setting, and state where recusal would be required.

bands.K–2: Tell an adult if you might be treated differently because you know someone.
bands.3–5: Notice when helping a friend might be unfair to others, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Identify a real conflict of interest, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Recognise and disclose a real conflict of interest, on your own.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else how to identify and handle a real conflict of interest.

themes.description: What may be accepted, what obligates, and the favor economy that corrupts by inches.
themes.transfer_check: For three real scenarios from your own context, rule accept/decline/disclose with reasons, and check them against any written code that applies.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult if it's okay to accept a gift for doing a job.
bands.3–5: Learn why accepting gifts for favors can be a problem, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Identify a real inappropriate gift or favor, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Navigate a real gift or favor situation ethically, on your own.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else the real rules around gifts and favors in public life.

themes.description: The friend, the boss, the party — where loyalty ends and complicity begins, decided before the moment arrives.
themes.transfer_check: Write your own loyalty lines for your real roles — what you would refuse whom — and test one against a case study honestly.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult what to do if a friend does something wrong.
bands.3–5: Learn that loyalty has limits when something is wrong, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Identify a real point where loyalty must yield to ethics, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Recognise a real limit to loyalty in an ethical dilemma, on your own.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else where real loyalty's limit actually is.

themes.description: Disagreeing upward and inward — the loyal dissent that improves decisions, delivered so it can be heard.
themes.transfer_check: Deliver one real dissent to a decision your own group favors — in the room, on the record — and report its reception and result.

bands.K–2: Say you disagree with a friend's plan kindly, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Voice disagreement with a team's plan respectfully, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Voice real dissent within a real team appropriately, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Voice real dissent within a real team while staying constructive, on your own.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else how to handle real dissent inside a team well.

themes.description: When internal dissent is exhausted — the escalation ladder, its protections where you live, and its real costs.
themes.transfer_check: For a case-study wrong, map the full escalation ladder in your jurisdiction — internal to external — with each step's protections and risks.

bands.K–2: Tell an adult right away if something seems very wrong.
bands.3–5: Report a real serious problem to a trusted adult, with their help.
bands.6–8: Recognise a real situation that requires whistleblowing, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Recognise and respond to a real whistleblowing situation appropriately.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else the real weight and protections of whistleblowing.

themes.description: The affirmative-push principle as ethics — spending your own access on those the ceiling still holds down.
themes.transfer_check: Spend one real unit of your own access — an introduction, a nomination, a platform — on someone blocked, documented with their consent.

bands.K–2: Help a friend who is being left out, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Use your position to help someone who's stuck, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Use real influence to help someone who is blocked, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Use your own real influence to help someone genuinely blocked, on your own.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else why real power should serve the blocked, not the powerful.

themes.description: Accountability as practice — reporting back to the people affected, in their room, before they ask.
themes.transfer_check: After one real responsibility you held, deliver the unprompted account to those affected — what you did, what went wrong, what changes.

bands.K–2: Explain to an adult why you made a choice.
bands.3–5: Explain your real decision to someone affected by it, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Give a real account of a real decision to those it affects, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Give a real account of your decisions to those affected, on your own.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else why real leaders owe an account of their decisions.

themes.description: The capstone: your own record read the way you read a leader's — honestly, with the principles as the measure.
themes.transfer_check: Write the honest review of your own service record to date against the twelve principles, and set one measurable correction.

bands.K–2: Think about whether you were fair to a friend, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Reflect on whether a real choice you made was fair, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Reflect honestly on a real past decision's ethics, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Regularly examine your own real decisions for their ethics, on your own.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else why a real career needs regular ethical examination.
